presentingComplaint: Progressive drowsiness and reduced oral intake over 6 days, on the 4th post-operative day after a right hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur.
history: A 78-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes (on metformin and gliclazide), hypertension and osteoarthritis was admitted 4 days ago following a fall and underwent right hemiarthroplasty. Recovery was complicated by poor mobilisation and reduced appetite. She was commenced on a short reducing course of dexamethasone for post-operative nausea and remained on her regular bendroflumethiazide and a recently added NSAID for pain. Nursing staff noted increasing thirst, high-volume urine output in the catheter bag and, over the last 48 hours, escalating confusion and lethargy. She has had no fever, cough, dysuria or diarrhoea. Family report she has been drinking sweetened supplement drinks to 'keep her strength up'. Capillary glucose meters had been reading 'HI' since yesterday but were not escalated. No history of insulin use, no vomiting of note, no chest or abdominal pain.
examination: Elderly woman, obtunded but rousable to voice, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5). Profoundly dehydrated: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, capillary refill 4 seconds. No focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, pupils equal and reactive. No asterixis, no ketotic fetor. Chest clear, heart sounds normal, no murmur. Abdomen soft, surgical wound clean and dry with no surrounding erythema or discharge. Calves soft and non-tender. Peripheries cool with thready pulses.
imaging: Chest radiograph clear with no consolidation. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemic changes. No CT head indicated given non-focal exam and osmolar explanation for reduced consciousness.
microbiology: Blood cultures, urine culture and wound swab sent to exclude an occult precipitant; no organism isolated and inflammatory markers only mildly raised. No antimicrobial indicated on current evidence.
finalDiagnosis: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state precipitated by post-operative dexamethasone, thiazide diuretic, high sugar oral intake and reduced free-water access in an elderly type 2 diabetic
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
JBDS-IP - The Management of the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults, 2022
ADA - Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes: A Consensus Report, 2024
stewardship: Non-infective metabolic emergency. Despite the acute illness there is no clinical, radiographic or laboratory evidence of infection (afebrile, WBC normal, CRP only mildly raised, cultures negative) and empiric antibiotics are not warranted; the precipitant is iatrogenic/metabolic (steroid, thiazide, hyperosmolar oral intake). Antibiotic stewardship priority here is to actively withhold reflexive empiric antimicrobials while investigating for an occult precipitant and to review the polypharmacy that provoked the crisis.
contraindications: Avoid rapid correction of serum sodium/osmolality (>10 mmol/L Na or >3 mOsm/kg/h fall) - risk of cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination

Do not give aggressive fixed-rate insulin before/while volume resuscitating - insulin alone shifts water intracellularly and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse; fluids first, low fixed-rate insulin only once glucose stops falling with fluids or ketones are significant
Withhold nephrotoxic and precipitating agents: NSAID, thiazide, metformin (in AKI), and taper the dexamethasone
Cautious potassium replacement guided by renal function given AKI
edgeCases: Overlap syndrome: mild ketonaemia/acidosis can coexist with HHS in the elderly, but effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg with glucose >30 mmol/L defines the HHS-predominant picture here
Corrected sodium is markedly high (158) - hypernatraemic dehydration masquerading as a primary sodium disorder
Steroid- and thiazide-induced hyperglycaemia is a classic reversible precipitant that is easily missed on a surgical ward
Mortality in HHS is substantially higher than DKA; VTE risk is high and prophylactic anticoagulation is indicated once bleeding risk assessed
expectedMaiK: Elderly post-operative type 2 diabetic on steroids/thiazide with obtundation, extreme hyperglycaemia (glucose >33 mmol/L), effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg and only trace ketones/no significant acidosis - hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, not DKA; manage with cautious IV 0.9% saline, controlled osmolality reduction, VTE prophylaxis and removal of precipitants.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the calculated effective serum osmolality and corrected sodium?
Are blood ketones and venous pH in the DKA range or is this hyperosmolar-predominant?
What new drugs (steroids, thiazides) and oral intake changes occurred post-operatively?
Is there an occult precipitant (silent infection, ACS, thromboembolism) despite absent fever?
What is the trajectory of renal function and urine output?
expectedInvestigations: U&E with corrected sodium and potassium
Blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate) and venous blood gas
ECG and troponin to exclude silent ACS as precipitant
Septic screen (cultures, CXR) to exclude occult infection

investigations: Blood ketones and venous blood gas

regressionAssertions: Effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg with glucose >30 mmol/L and only trace ketones must classify as HHS, not DKA
Must NOT recommend empiric antibiotics in the absence of infective evidence (afebrile, normal WBC, negative cultures)
Must prioritise cautious IV fluid resuscitation before/with low fixed-rate insulin and controlled osmolality reduction
Must flag steroid, thiazide and hyperosmolar oral intake as reversible precipitants and recommend VTE prophylaxis
